_summary: Master schema definition for all concept JSON files. Every concept page on the platform must follow this exact structure. This is the contract between the content and the React component that renders it.

_instructions.note: This file is documentation only — it is never imported by the app.
_instructions.rule_1: Every field marked required: true must be present in every concept file.
_instructions.rule_2: Arrays marked required: true must have at least one item.
_instructions.rule_3: Fields marked required: false can be omitted if not applicable to the concept.
_instructions.rule_4: The 'id' must match the filename exactly, e.g. file mean-median-mode.json → id: mean-median-mode
_instructions.rule_5: The 'section' value must exactly match one of the allowed section slugs listed below.
_instructions.rule_6: The 'color' value must exactly match one of the allowed pastel keys listed below.
_instructions.rule_7: Keep 'what_it_is' under 3 sentences — it is shown as a summary card on the section page.
_instructions.rule_8: The 'formula' field is optional — not every concept has one. Omit it cleanly if not needed.
_instructions.rule_9: related_concepts must reference valid IDs of other concepts that already exist.

_allowed_colors.yellow: warnings / exceptions / when NOT to use

id.description: Unique slug for this concept. Must match the filename without .json extension.

title.description: Display name shown as the page heading.

section.description: Which section this concept belongs to. Must be one of the allowed section slugs.

difficulty.description: Difficulty level — controls the badge shown on the concept card.

color.description: Pastel accent color used for the highlight boxes on this concept page.

tagline.description: One sentence shown under the title. Should answer: what is this in plain English? Think of it as the subtitle on a book cover.
tagline.example: Three ways to describe the center of your data — and why they disagree.

what_it_is.description: Plain English explanation of the concept. Max 3 sentences. No jargon unless immediately explained. This is the blue box on the concept page.
what_it_is.example: The mean is the sum of all values divided by how many there are. The median is the middle value when sorted. The mode is the value that appears most often.

why_it_exists.description: What problem this concept was invented to solve. Why do we need it? What breaks without it? This is the green box.
why_it_exists.example: A single number to represent a whole dataset is useful for comparison, communication and decision-making — but different measures protect against different distortions in the data.

what_it_measures.description: What this concept actually tells you about your data. What does the number/result represent in reality?
what_it_measures.example: Each measure tells you where most of your data sits — the center of gravity of the distribution. They differ in how much weight they give to extreme values.

intuition.description: A concrete analogy, story, or example that makes the concept click. Avoid abstract descriptions — use real scenarios. This is the most important field for understanding.
intuition.example: Imagine 5 friends earn: 20k, 22k, 21k, 23k, 200k. The mean is 57.2k — misleading because of the outlier. The median is 22k — a much truer picture of a typical salary in this group.

formula.description: Optional. Only include if a formula adds genuine understanding. Omit for purely conceptual topics. Written in LaTeX for KaTeX rendering.

breakdown.description: Each symbol explained in plain English. One object per symbol.

items.symbol: The symbol as it appears in the formula
items.means: What it represents in plain English

example.means: the mean — what we are calculating
how many values are in the dataset
each individual value in the dataset

when_to_use.description: List of specific situations where this concept is the right choice. Be concrete — name the scenario.
example: Use mean when data has no extreme outliers and follows a roughly normal distribution
Use median when data is skewed — e.g. income, house prices, response times
Use mode when data is categorical — e.g. most common product category, most frequent error code

when_not_to_use.description: Specific situations where this concept breaks, misleads, or is the wrong choice. This is the yellow warning box — it is what makes this platform different from a textbook.
example: Do not use mean with heavily skewed data — one outlier can make the mean unrepresentative of everyone else
Do not use mode as the only summary for continuous data — values rarely repeat exactly
Do not report only one measure — always consider all three together before choosing

common_mistakes.description: Mistakes people actually make with this concept in real DS work. Not theoretical errors — real ones.
example: Using mean salary to describe a company's compensation without checking for executive pay outliers
Assuming mean and median are always close — they diverge significantly in skewed distributions
Ignoring the mode entirely when analyzing customer behavior data

ds_usage.description: How and where this concept appears specifically in Data Science work. Name the real tasks, tools, or model types where it comes up.
ds_usage.example: Used in EDA to understand data distribution before modeling. Pandas provides mean(), median() and mode() directly on Series. Choosing the wrong central tendency for imputing missing values can silently bias your entire model.

related_concepts.description: IDs of other concepts on the platform that connect to this one. Used to render the related links at the bottom of each page. Only reference concepts that actually exist.

key_points.description: 3 to 5 bullet points summarising the most important things to remember. Used as the quick-revision box at the top of the page. Future use: interview questions will be generated from these.
example: Mean = sum divided by count. Sensitive to outliers.
Median = middle value. Robust to outliers. Use for skewed data.
Mode = most frequent value. Only meaningful measure for categorical data.
In a perfectly normal distribution, mean = median = mode.
Always check all three before deciding which to report.
